claim: Bacteria were detected in egg jellies across all developmental stages of Ranitomeya variabilis embryos.
source: Bacteria were detected in egg jellies across all developmental stages (formation of the dorsal lip to hatchling) but were not detected in embryos prior to hatching from the vitelline membrane (N=12) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by broad-range PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene and visualization on agarose gel.

claim: Bacteria were not detected in Ranitomeya variabilis embryos prior to hatching from the vitelline membrane.
source: Bacteria were detected in egg jellies across all developmental stages (formation of the dorsal lip to hatchling) but were not detected in embryos prior to hatching from the vitelline membrane (N=12) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by broad-range PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene showing no amplification in unhatched embryos.

claim: After hatching, bacteria were detected in Ranitomeya variabilis tadpoles that remained in the jelly and in tadpoles that were transported by their caregiver.
source: After hatching, bacteria were detected in tadpoles that remained in the jelly and in tadpoles that were transported by their caregiver (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by broad-range PCR targeting the 16S rRNA gene.

claim: Unhatched Ranitomeya variabilis embryos contained on average 2942 copies of the 16S rRNA gene per µl.
source: We found that unhatched embryos contained on average 2942 copies of the 16 S rRNA gene per µl (min = 742, max = 11584, std = ± 3086)
evidence: Measured using droplet digital PCR (ddPCR).

claim: Egg jellies of Ranitomeya variabilis contained on average 6128 times as many 16S rRNA gene copies as unhatched embryos.
source: while jellies contained on average 6128 times as many (min = 457417, max = 66115451, mean = 18029604 ± 18586471; Kruskal-Wallis (KW): chi-squared=18.6667, df = 2, p<0.00001) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Measured using droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) and compared with Kruskal-Wallis test.

claim: 16S rRNA gene copy concentrations were on average 8310 times higher in hatched relative to unhatched Ranitomeya variabilis embryos.
source: 16 S rRNA gene copy concentrations were on average 8310 times higher in hatched relative to unhatched embryos (min = 737340, max = 48159335, mean = 24448337 ± 33532414; KW: p=0.0195)
evidence: Measured using droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) and compared with Kruskal-Wallis test.

claim: 16S rRNA gene copy concentrations in hatched Ranitomeya variabilis embryos did not differ significantly from concentrations detected in the jelly.
source: but did not differ significantly from concentrations detected in the jelly (KW: p=0.5) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: Compared using Kruskal-Wallis test on ddPCR data.

claim: Transporting frogs serve as a source of skin microbes for tadpoles on their back.
source: A cross-foster experiment demonstrated that poison frogs performing tadpole transport serve as a source of skin microbes for tadpoles on their back.
evidence: Demonstrated through cross-foster experiment where tadpoles transported by heterospecific frogs (Oophaga sylvatica) shared higher proportions of their communities with the transporting species than with the biological parent species.

claim: Bacterial community composition on caregiver skin was primarily shaped by host species (Ranitomeya variabilis versus Oophaga sylvatica).
source: We found that bacterial community composition on caregiver skin was primarily shaped by host species (Rv versus Os; Adonis: Bray-Curtis: F1, 12 = 5.6538, R2=0.33949, p=0.001; unweighted Unifrac: F1, 12 = 2.0078, R2=0.15435, p=0.013)
evidence: Analyzed using PERMANOVA on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data with Bray-Curtis and Unifrac distances.

claim: After 6 hours of being carried on the back, bacterial community composition on Ranitomeya variabilis tadpole skin was influenced by caregiving species.
source: Indeed, we found that after 6 hr of being carried on the back, bacterial community composition on Rv tadpole skin was influenced by caregiving species (Rv versus Os; Adonis: Bray-Curtis: F1, 12 = 1.75, R2=0.099, p=0.017; Unifrac: F1, 12 = 1.67, R2=0.095, p=0.015).
evidence: Analyzed using PERMANOVA on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Tadpoles transported by Oophaga sylvatica always shared a higher proportion of their communities with this heterospecific caregiver than siblings that were not transported.
source: Tadpoles of a clutch that were transported by Os always shared a higher proportion of their communities with this heterospecific caregiver than siblings that were not transported (KW: chi2=14.4696, df = 2, p=0.0003; difference in proportion: median = 39.33, min = 0.872%, max = 68.478%)
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data and compared with Kruskal-Wallis test.

claim: Tadpoles transported by Oophaga sylvatica shared a higher proportion of their communities with this heterospecific caregiver than siblings transported by the biological parent.
source: or siblings transported by the biological parent (KW: p=0.015; percentage of higher proportion: median = 37.07%, min = 0.874 %, max = 72.97%) (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis and compared with Kruskal-Wallis test.

claim: All but two transported tadpoles shared a larger proportion of their communities with the transporting species than with the non-transporting species.
source: Similarly, all but two transported tadpoles shared a larger proportion of their communities with the transporting species than with the non-transporting species (p=0.001) (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Transported tadpoles generally shared higher proportions of their skin communities with the transporting species than did non-transported tadpoles.
source: Transported tadpoles (N=18) generally shared higher proportions of their skin communities with the transporting species than did non-transported tadpoles (N=6) (Kruskal-Wallis chi2=19.4029, df = 2, p=0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis and compared with Kruskal-Wallis test.

claim: Non-transported tadpoles were colonized by between 5 and 57 Amplicon Sequence Variants (median = 12).
source: Non-transported tadpoles were colonized by between 5 and 57 Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) (median = 12).
evidence: Determined from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Transported tadpoles shared between 0 and 46.99% (median = 13%) of their communities with non-transported tadpoles.
source: We found that transported tadpoles shared between 0 and 46.99% (median = 13%) of their communities with non-transported tadpoles.
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis defining non-transported tadpoles as potential microbe sources.

claim: Sourcetracker detected higher proportions of clutch-acquired microbes in tadpoles transported by Oophaga sylvatica.
source: Sourcetracker detected higher proportions of clutch-acquired microbes in tadpoles transported by Os (pairwise Wilcoxon test, p=0.02).
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis and compared with pairwise Wilcoxon test.

claim: ASVs belonging to Phylum Proteobacteria dominated the microbial community across all species and life stages (mean relative abundance: 70.9%).
source: As previously reported for Neotropical frogs (Hughey et al., 2017), ASVs belonging to Phylum Proteobacteria dominated the microbial community across all species and life stages (mean relative abundance: 70.9%), followed by Bacteroidota (10.3%), Actinobacteriota (4.1%), Firmicutes (4%), Verrucomicrobiota (2.3%), and Planctomycetota (1.1%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Determined from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data of wild populations; also supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The abundance of the frog pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) in the rock savanna was low.
source: The abundance of the frog pathogen Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis (Bd) in the rock savanna was low, with detection in two samples of Rv adults and one Rv tadpole, but no positive Ll sample.
evidence: Based on detection in samples from wild populations.

claim: Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis was detected on one adult Allobates femoralis individual collected in primary forest but not on tadpoles of this species collected in the same area.
source: We detected Bd on one adult Af individual collected in primary forest but not on tadpoles of this species collected in the same area.
evidence: Based on detection in samples from wild populations.

claim: In all species, tadpole communities contained fewer taxa with known Batrachochytrium-growth inhibiting function than did environmental samples or adults.
source: In all species, tadpole communities contained fewer taxa with known Batrachochytrium-growth inhibiting function than did environmental samples or adults (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Determined by blasting the dataset against the AmphiBac-Database-2023.2.

claim: There were no significant differences in the observed ASV richness, diversity (Shannon), or evenness between tadpoles and adults of the poison frogs Ranitomeya variabilis and Allobates femoralis.
source: We found no significant differences in the observed ASV richness, diversity (Shannon), or evenness between tadpoles and adults of the poison frogs Rv and Af.
evidence: Analyzed using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test on rarefied 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Leptodactylus longirostris tadpoles were significantly less diverse than Leptodactylus longirostris adults.
source: In contrast, Ll tadpoles were significantly less diverse than Ll adults (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Analyzed using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test on rarefied 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Ranitomeya variabilis and Allobates femoralis tadpoles had higher microbial diversity and evenness compared to Leptodactylus longirostris tadpoles.
source: We followed up on this finding by comparing the diversity of tadpole-associated communities across species and found higher microbial diversity and evenness in Rv and Af tadpoles compared to Ll tadpoles (Figure 2C).
evidence: Analyzed using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test on rarefied 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Microbial communities associated with Ranitomeya variabilis aquatic environments were less diverse and even compared to those in Allobates femoralis and Leptodactylus longirostris habitats.
source: Differences in community diversity of tadpoles were not a reflection of habitat diversity: microbial communities associated with Rv aquatic environments were less diverse and even compared to those in Af and Ll habitats (Figure 2D).
evidence: Analyzed using ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis test on rarefied 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Tadpoles of all species clustered separately from adults, each other, and their aquatic environment.
source: Tadpoles of all species clustered separately from adults, each other, and their aquatic environment (PERMANOVA on genus level, df = 8, R2=0.52909, F=18.117, p adj = 0.001) (Figure 3A and B; Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Analyzed using PERMANOVA on Bray-Curtis dissimilarities from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Skin communities varied significantly across life stages in all species.
source: Consistent with findings in pond-spawning anurans (Kueneman et al., 2014; Prest et al., 2018), skin communities varied significantly across life stages in all species (PERMANOVA on genus level: species: df = 5, R2=0.29674, F=11.139, p=0.001, life stage: df = 2, R2=0.23148, F=20.331, p=0.001).
evidence: Analyzed using PERMANOVA on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data; also supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Parental care explained some of the observed variance in skin microbial communities.
source: Parental care also explained some of the observed variance (PERMANOVA on genus level: df = 2, R2=0.07513, F=5.4831, p=0.001).
evidence: Analyzed using PERMANOVA on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Independent of parenting strategy and species, tadpoles shared core communities of their microbiome with their environments, but not with adult individuals.
source: Independent of parenting strategy and species, tadpoles shared core communities of their microbiome with their environments, but not with adult individuals.
evidence: Determined by comparing core communities across a range of prevalence and abundance cutoffs from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Adult poison frogs never shared core taxa with the aquatic environment of their tadpoles.
source: Adult poison frogs never shared core taxa with the aquatic environment of their tadpoles (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1f), even though adults were commonly found in the nurseries.
evidence: Determined by comparing core communities from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: The aquatic environment contributed substantially to the skin community of adult Leptodactylus longirostris.
source: In contrast, the aquatic environment contributed substantially to the skin community of adult Ll, which shared high- and low-abundance (≥0.1%) core genera with the pond water, but not with the pond-inhabiting tadpoles (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Determined by comparing core communities from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: There was no difference in community distances between tadpoles and adults in Allobates femoralis and Leptodactylus longirostris.
source: We found no difference in community distances between tadpoles and adults in Af and Ll (iterated beta regression averaged over 999 random subsamples of similar sample size (IBR): Unifrac: p=0.3).
evidence: Analyzed using iterated beta regression on Unifrac distances from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Communities associated with Ranitomeya variabilis tadpoles were more dissimilar from adult communities than microbiota of Leptodactylus longirostris tadpoles and adults.
source: Communities associated with Rv tadpoles were more dissimilar from adult communities than microbiota of Ll tadpoles and adults (IBR: Unifrac: p=0.008).
evidence: Analyzed using iterated beta regression on Unifrac distances from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Microbes acquired during tadpole transport do not create lasting similarities in composition between tadpoles and adults of wild populations.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that microbes acquired during tadpole transport do not create lasting similarities in composition between tadpoles and adults of wild populations.
evidence: Inferred from beta regression analysis showing no higher similarity between tadpoles and adults in transporting species compared to non-transporting species.

claim: Richness and evenness of tadpole communities did not differ significantly between transported and non-transported experimental conditions.
source: Richness and evenness of tadpole communities did not differ significantly between experimental conditions (ANOVA: Observed ASVs: df = 1, F=2.7234, p.adj=0.3552; Shannon: df = 1, F=1.2067, p.adj=0.8646; evenness: df = 1, F=0.0009, p.adj=2.9313)
evidence: Analyzed using ANOVA on rarefied 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data from field experiment.

claim: PCoA on Unifrac distances revealed differences in microbiome composition attributable to the presence or absence of transport in the field experiment.
source: though PCoA on Unifrac distances revealed differences in microbiome composition attributable to the presence or absence of transport (Figure 4B) (PERMANOVA: df = 1, R2=0.11759, F=2.1321, p=0.002).
evidence: Analyzed using PERMANOVA on Unifrac distances from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Compared to transported tadpoles, non-transported tadpoles showed less overlap of genera in their microbial community with their aquatic environment.
source: Compared to transported tadpoles, non-transported tadpoles showed less overlap of genera in their microbial community with their aquatic environment (Figure 4C).
evidence: Determined by comparing genus-level ASVs from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: The genera Pelomonas, Rhodomicrobium (Proteobacteria), Mycobacterium (Actinobacteriota), and Candidatus Koribacter (Acidobacteriota) primarily colonized transported tadpoles.
source: Specifically, the genera Pelomonas, Rhodomicrobium (Proteobacteria), Mycobacterium (Actinobacteriota), and Candidatus Koribacter (Acidobacteriota) primarily colonized transported tadpoles, while the genus Limnohabitans (Proteobacteria) was found on non-transported tadpoles.
evidence: Determined using ANCOMBC 2 analysis on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: The genus Limnohabitans (Proteobacteria) was found on non-transported tadpoles.
source: Specifically, the genera Pelomonas, Rhodomicrobium (Proteobacteria), Mycobacterium (Actinobacteriota), and Candidatus Koribacter (Acidobacteriota) primarily colonized transported tadpoles, while the genus Limnohabitans (Proteobacteria) was found on non-transported tadpoles.
evidence: Determined using ANCOMBC 2 analysis on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Cetobacterium and Burkholderia-Caballeronia-Paraburkholderia were found to colonize tadpoles from both experimental conditions, but at different abundances.
source: Cetobacterium and Burkholderia-Caballeronia-Paraburkholderia were found to colonize tadpoles from both experimental conditions, but at different abundances (ANCOMBC 2, p<0.05; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Determined using ANCOMBC 2 analysis on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: One month after transport, skin communities of tadpoles were not more similar to the transporting parent than to unrelated adults of the population.
source: One month after transport, we found that skin communities of tadpoles were not more similar to the transporting parent than to unrelated adults of the population (iterated beta regression averaged over 999 random subsamples of similar sample size (N=10) (IBR): Unifrac: p=0.27)
evidence: Analyzed using iterated beta regression on Unifrac distances from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: A Sourcetracker analysis revealed notable relative contributions of the parental skin community to the community on four transported tadpoles (tadpoles 1, 2, 6, 8).
source: However, a Sourcetracker analysis on unrarefied data revealed notable relative contributions of the parental skin community to the community on four transported tadpoles (tadpoles 1, 2, 6, 8) (min = 0% to max = 17%, median = 0%, IQR = 10.5; Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Determined using Sourcetracker analysis on 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: 8 out of 10 tadpoles shared one or two ASVs with the frog that had transported them in relative abundances ranging from 0.02 to 19.3%.
source: We found that 8 out of 10 tadpoles shared one or two ASVs with the frog that had transported them in relative abundances ranging from 0.02 to 19.3% (Figure 4D; Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Determined by identifying shared ASVs from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Shared taxa between transported tadpoles and their caregivers belong to the genera Akkermansia, Elsteraceae, Aquitalea, Methylocella, Methylobacterium-Methylorubrum, Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas, and Acinetobacter.
source: Shared taxa belong to the genera Akkermansia, Elsteraceae, Aquitalea, Methylocella, Methylobacterium-Methylorubrum, Staphylococcus, Pseudomonas, and Acinetobacter.
evidence: Determined by identifying shared ASVs from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Seven out of ten shared microbes constituted members of the ten most abundant ASVs found on the respective transporting frog.
source: Seven out of ten shared microbes constituted members of the ten most abundant ASVs found on the respective transporting frog (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: Determined from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Absolute abundances of shared ASVs likely originating from the parental source pool after one month of growth ranged from 7804–172,326 sequence copies per tadpole.
source: Absolute abundances of shared ASVs likely originating from the parental source pool (as identified by Sourcetracker) after one month of growth ranged from 7804–172,326 sequence copies per tadpole (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Calculated by multiplying 16S rRNA gene copy numbers from dPCR by relative abundances from amplicon sequencing.

claim: At least six of the ten ASVs shared between caregivers and transported tadpoles were consistently present in the aquatic environment of non-transported experimental tadpoles.
source: Even though at least six (min: 6, avg: 6.38, max: 7) of the ten ASVs were consistently present in the aquatic environment of non-transported experimental tadpoles, only one (family Enterobacteriaceae) successfully colonized their skin (Figure 4D, not transported tadpoles; Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Determined from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Only one ASV (family Enterobacteriaceae) that was present in the aquatic environment successfully colonized the skin of non-transported tadpoles.
source: Even though at least six (min: 6, avg: 6.38, max: 7) of the ten ASVs were consistently present in the aquatic environment of non-transported experimental tadpoles, only one (family Enterobacteriaceae) successfully colonized their skin (Figure 4D, not transported tadpoles; Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: Determined from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing data.

claim: Vertical transmission may be a more effective mode of transmission of host-adapted microbes compared to horizontal transmission from the environment.
source: These results suggest that vertical transmission may be a more effective mode of transmission of host-adapted microbes compared to horizontal transmission from the environment.
evidence: Inferred from observation that most ASVs shared between caregivers and transported tadpoles failed to colonize non-transported hosts despite being present in their aquatic environment.

claim: Early microbial colonizers shape community structure of newborns in insects, mammals, fish, birds, and anurans via priority effects.
source: Early microbial colonizers have been shown to shape community structure of newborns in insects (Jones et al., 2022), mammals (Blyton et al., 2022; Kaur et al., 2022; Sprockett et al., 2018), fish (Almany, 2004), birds (Chen et al., 2020), and anurans (Jones et al., 2024; Jones et al., 2023) via priority effects (see Debray et al., 2022; Fukami, 2015 for reviews).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Inoculation of embryos has been shown to increase the relative abundance of beneficial taxa such as Janthinobacterium lividum in tadpoles.
source: For example, inoculation of embryos has been shown to increase the relative abundance of beneficial taxa such as Janthinobacterium lividum in tadpoles (Jones et al., 2024)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Efforts to introduce Janthinobacterium lividum into established adult frog communities have not led to long-term persistence.
source: whereas efforts to introduce the same organism into established adult communities have not led to long-term persistence (Bletz, 2013; Woodhams et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The vitelline membrane may function as a selective barrier in anuran embryos, permitting the passage of certain taxa.
source: Alternatively, the vitelline membrane may function as a selective barrier, permitting the passage of certain taxa, with hosts acting as additional filter to select suitable colonizers.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms based on observed data.

claim: The avian vitelline membrane has a barrier function mediated by antimicrobial proteins.
source: For example, the latter was described for the avian vitelline membrane, where it is mediated by antimicrobial proteins (Guyot et al., 2016; Mann, 2008; Mine and Kovacs-Nolan, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The amphibian symbiont Oophila amblystomatis is acquired by oviductal transmission and grows on the inside of individual salamander and frog vitelline membranes.
source: Those bacteria that are present in unhatched tadpoles might have been acquired prior to hatching, such as in the case of the amphibian symbiont Oophila amblystomatis (Kerney et al., 2011), which is acquired by oviductal transmission and grows on the inside of individual salamander and frog vitelline membranes.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Previous studies in anurans investigating vertical transmission of microbes during egg attendance did not find evidence for parental inoculation.
source: Previous studies in anurans have investigated vertical transmission of microbes during parental care in the context of indirect transmission during egg attendance without considering less widespread parenting strategies involving direct parental contact. These studies did not find evidence for parental inoculation, as hatched tadpoles supported bacterial communities very similar to adult frogs but independent of caregiver identity (Hughey et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Both clutch environment and transporting caregivers can serve as a source pool for hatched tadpoles.
source: Thus, in this clade, both clutch environment and transporting caregivers can serve as a source pool for hatched tadpoles.
evidence: Inferred from cross-foster experiment results showing tadpoles share microbes with both clutch siblings and transporting frogs.

claim: Duration of tadpole transport might influence microbial acquisition in a time-dependent manner.
source: Prolonged parental care has been shown to enhance the generational transmission of symbiotic microorganisms in burying beetles (e.g. Körner et al., 2023) and thus, duration of the skin-to-skin contact during tadpoles transport might influence microbial acquisition in a time-dependent manner.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on citation to previous work in other organisms.

claim: Early life microbes are introduced to the poison frog host in a mixed transmission mode, where community members can be sourced environmentally from the egg jelly and socially from a caregiving frog.
source: Collectively, our findings suggest that early life microbes are introduced to the poison frog host in a mixed transmission mode, where community members can be sourced environmentally from the egg jelly and socially from a caregiving frog.
evidence: Inferred from cross-foster experiment and field experiment results.

claim: Kouete et al. documented the first case of vertical transmission in amphibians, observed in subterranean caecilians that protect and feed their offspring.
source: Recent evidence from Kouete et al. documented the first case of vertical transmission in amphibians, observed in subterranean caecilians that protect and feed their offspring Kouete et al., 2023.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: This is the first study that extends evidence for vertical transmission during parental care to the order of anurans.
source: To our knowledge, ours is the first study that extends evidence for vertical transmission during parental care to the order of anurans.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their experimental results.

claim: While poison frog tadpoles do acquire caregiver-specific microbes during transport, most of these microbes do not persist on the tadpoles' skin long-term.
source: While poison frog tadpoles do acquire caregiver-specific microbes during transport, most of these microbes do not persist on the tadpoles' skin long-term.
evidence: Inferred from field experiment and population sampling showing no higher similarity between caregivers and tadpoles compared to unrelated adults after one month.

claim: The limited persistence of transmitted microbes can likely be attributed to the capacity of tadpole skin and gut microbiota to flexibly adapt to environmental changes.
source: This pattern can likely be attributed to the capacity of tadpole skin and gut microbiota to flexibly adapt to environmental changes (Emerson and Woodley, 2024; Santos et al., 2023; Scarberry et al., 2024).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The limited persistence of transmitted microbes may reflect the limited compatibility of skin microbiota from terrestrial adults with aquatic habitats or tadpole skin.
source: It may also reflect the limited compatibility of skin microbiota from terrestrial adults with aquatic habitats or tadpole skin, which differs structurally from that of adults (Faszewski et al., 2008).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Many transmitted microbes are probably outcompeted by microbial taxa continuously supplied by the aquatic environment.
source: As a result, many transmitted microbes are probably outcompeted by microbial taxa continuously supplied by the aquatic environment.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed patterns.

claim: Adult Leptodactylus longirostris commonly inhabit the rock pools where their tadpoles develop.
source: This pattern might reflect differences in life history among the species. Adult Ll commonly inhabit the rock pools where their tadpoles develop, but adults of the two poison frog species visit tadpole nurseries only sporadically for deposition.
evidence: Based on knowledge of species natural history.

claim: Adults of Ranitomeya variabilis and Allobates femoralis visit tadpole nurseries only sporadically for deposition.
source: This pattern might reflect differences in life history among the species. Adult Ll commonly inhabit the rock pools where their tadpoles develop, but adults of the two poison frog species visit tadpole nurseries only sporadically for deposition.
evidence: Based on knowledge of species natural history.

claim: Differences in habitat use may result in adult Leptodactylus longirostris hosting skin microbiota that are better adapted to aquatic environments as compared to Ranitomeya variabilis and Allobates femoralis.
source: These differences in habitat use may result in adult Ll hosting skin microbiota that are better adapted to aquatic environments as compared to Rv and Af.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on observed patterns and life history differences.

claim: The presence of adult Leptodactylus longirostris in the tadpoles' habitat could make them a more consistent source of microbiota for developing tadpoles.
source: Additionally, their presence in the tadpoles' habitat could make Ll a more consistent source of microbiota for developing tadpoles.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on life history differences.

claim: Transient shifts in the composition of tadpole-associated communities followed by later convergence have been observed in wood frogs experimentally inoculated with bullfrog gut microbes.
source: Transient shifts in the composition of tadpole-associated communities followed by later convergence have also been observed in wood frogs experimentally inoculated with bullfrog gut microbes (Warne et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Despite compositional convergence in wood frogs, effects of early microbial disruption on host physiology and disease susceptibility persisted.
source: Notably, despite this compositional convergence, effects of early microbial disruption on host physiology and disease susceptibility persisted- an outcome also documented in fruit flies (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vertically acquired microbes may durably imprint the immune system of poison frogs.
source: Therefore, it is possible that vertically acquired microbes shape communities of poison frogs in different ways than by gaining abundance priority on tadpole skin. For example, they may durably imprint the immune system (Fallet et al., 2022; Gensollen et al., 2016)
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vertically acquired microbes may alter host metabolic phenotypes in poison frogs.
source: and alter host metabolic phenotypes (Cox et al., 2014; Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013).
evidence: Speculative reasoning supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low-abundant keystone taxa can act as drivers of compositional changes despite their rarity.
source: There is clear evidence that low-abundant keystone taxa, despite their rarity, can act as drivers of compositional changes (Han and Vaishnava, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Low abundance ASVs drive compositional changes in the hindgut of subterranean termites after dietary alterations.
source: For instance, low abundance ASVs drive compositional changes in the hindgut of subterranean termites after dietary alterations (Benjamino et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Low abundance ASVs confer resistance to Salmonella-induced colitis in mice.
source: and confer resistance to Salmonella-induced colitis in mice (Herp et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Skin alkaloids are found on many adult poison frogs including Ranitomeya variabilis and influence skin community composition.
source: Although skin alkaloids are found on many adult poison frogs including Rv and influence skin community composition (Caty et al., 2024b), they are not present on adult Af or on tadpoles of any species included in this study (Villanueva et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Skin alkaloids are not present on adult Allobates femoralis or on tadpoles of any species included in this study.
